tagline: Scattered atolls across the date line
overview:
Kiribati is made up of 33 low coral islands scattered across a stretch of the Pacific Ocean larger than India, though the land itself adds up to only about 811 km², roughly the size of New York City. The country straddles both the equator and the international date line, so parts of Kiribati are among the first places on Earth to begin each new day. The capital, South Tarawa, is a crowded strip of land on an atoll in the west.

About 130,000 people live in Kiribati, nearly all of them I-Kiribati, a Micronesian people. Gilbertese and English are the official languages, and the country is a republic. Fishing licenses sold to foreign fleets, coconut products, and wages sent home by sailors working on cargo ships support the economy. Almost all of the land lies less than three meters above the sea, so rising sea levels and stronger storms are an immediate danger rather than a distant worry.
landAndNature: Kiribati's islands are atolls: rings of coral reef around shallow lagoons, built up over sunken volcanoes. Because the ground is coral sand, soil is thin and poor, and fresh water sits in a fragile lens beneath the surface that salt water can easily spoil. Coconut palms, pandanus and breadfruit are the main plants, and the ocean supplies most food, with reefs full of parrotfish, giant clams and reef sharks. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area, one of the largest marine reserves on Earth, guards some of the least disturbed coral in the Pacific. Kiritimati, also called Christmas Island, is the world's largest coral atoll and a nesting place for millions of seabirds.
peopleAndCulture: Life in Kiribati revolves around the sea and the extended family. Islanders once navigated open ocean by stars, swells and the flight of birds, and outrigger canoes are still built and raced. The maneaba, a large open meeting house with a steep thatched roof, stands at the center of every village, where elders discuss decisions and everyone gathers for feasts. Dancing is sharp and precise, with sudden birdlike movements of the arms and head, performed to sung chanting. Fish, coconut, breadfruit and taro make up daily meals. Christianity is widely practiced, and powerful church singing is a central part of island life.
history: Austronesian voyagers settled these atolls roughly 3,000 years ago, and later arrivals from Samoa, Tonga and Fiji added to the culture. European ships sighted the islands in the 1700s and 1800s, and whalers and traders followed. Britain declared a protectorate over the Gilbert and Ellice Islands in 1892 and mined the island of Banaba for phosphate until it was nearly stripped bare. In November 1943 the atoll of Tarawa was the site of one of the fiercest battles of the Pacific war. The Ellice Islands later separated to become Tuvalu, and Kiribati became independent on July 12, 1979. Rising seas have been the country's central concern ever since.
funFacts: Kiribati's islands are spread across an ocean area larger than India, but all its land would fit inside New York City.
In 1995 Kiribati shifted the international date line eastward so the whole country would share one calendar day.
Kiritimati, or Christmas Island, is the largest coral atoll in the world measured by land area.
Most of Kiribati lies under three meters above sea level, so rising seas threaten homes and drinking water alike.
The Phoenix Islands Protected Area is one of the largest marine reserves on Earth, and almost nobody lives inside it.
